column4: `صِرَاطِي مُسْتَقِيمًا` is one road to follow, while `السُّبُل` split walkers away from it; it makes the requested common, straight track the opposite of dispersal.
`هَدَانِي ... إِلَىٰ صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ دِينًا قِيَمًا` explicitly brings guidance, the straight path, and an upright lived religion into one claim.
Moses is travelling toward Madyan and asks to be guided to `سَوَاءَ السَّبِيلِ`, staging the section's road-finding at the middle of a way.
Mountains, rivers, and `سُبُلًا لَّعَلَّكُمْ تَهْتَدُونَ` make a physical landscape in which routes exist so that people can find their way.
`عَلَامَاتٍ` and the star by which people `يَهْتَدُونَ` give the traveller's landmarks and navigation which the section hears beside `ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ`.
The person left `فِي الْأَرْضِ حَيْرَانَ` is called `إِلَى الْهُدَى` by companions, a full scene of the lost traveller and a community on the way.
`وَوَجَدَكَ ضَالًّا فَهَدَىٰ` puts being lost and being guided in the same reversal that frames the plea of 1:6 and its ending in `ٱلضَّآلِّينَ`.
Iblis vows to sit on `صِرَاطَكَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ`; the danger is placed directly upon the road whose guidance is sought.
The attack comes from front, back, right, and left, completing the preceding road-ambush as pressure from every side of a straight course.
`اعْبُدُونِي هَٰذَا صِرَاطٌ مُّسْتَقِيمٌ` makes worship itself the straight path, joining the movement from `نَعْبُدُ` to `ٱلصِّرَاط`.
Satan has `أَضَلَّ ... جِبِلًّا كَثِيرًا`; beside the command to worship, it shows a great human multitude diverted from that path.
Jesus says `فَاعْبُدُوهُ هَٰذَا صِرَاطٌ مُّسْتَقِيمٌ`, the same worship-as-road claim made in 36:61.
`فَاعْبُدُوهُ هَٰذَا صِرَاطٌ مُّسْتَقِيمٌ` again makes shared worship the road itself.
Jesus' command `فَاعْبُدُوهُ هَٰذَا صِرَاطٌ مُّسْتَقِيمٌ` joins service and the one straight course.
`فَاهْدُوهُمْ إِلَىٰ صِرَاطِ الْجَحِيمِ` reverses the requested guidance: the same leading and road vocabulary now reaches the Fire.
`ضَلَّ سَوَاءَ السَّبِيلِ` directly names losing the middle of the road, the inverse of remaining in the road's centre.
`وَعَلَى اللَّهِ قَصْدُ السَّبِيلِ` sets the right direction of the way against a way that is `جَائِرٌ`, making straightness and deviation properties of routes.
People are told not to sit at every road, threaten travellers, block God's way, and seek it crooked; it closely parallels Iblis stationed on the straight road.
Stars are made so people may be guided through the darknesses of land and sea, a navigation scene that supplements the landmarks and star of 16:16.
The earth has firm mountains and broad mountain-pass roads, `فِجَاجًا سُبُلًا`, so that people may be guided; paths are formed through terrain for travel.
The one who guides through land-and-sea darkness and sends winds is invoked; this is the traveller's disorientation answered by guidance through signs.
God made the earth a resting ground and placed `سُبُلًا` through it, giving the section's path a made, traversable ground.
God made paths in the earth `لَعَلَّكُمْ تَهْتَدُونَ`; the route and the act of finding it occur together.
The earth is made `ذَلُولًا` and people are told to walk its tracts; its subdued walking-ground vividly answers the commentary's softened, traversable path.
God makes the earth a spread-out ground, furnishing the surface on which the following ayah's broad roads can be travelled.
`لِتَسْلُكُوا مِنْهَا سُبُلًا فِجَاجًا` makes human walking on broad roads the purpose of the spread earth in the preceding ayah.
The bee is commanded to follow the ways of its Lord, `سُبُلَ رَبِّكِ ذُلُلًا`; paths are expressly made easy to be traversed.
God calls to `دَارِ السَّلَامِ` and guides whom He wills to a straight path, joining the destination-home to the guidance that reaches it.
The ayah asks whether the one who guides to truth is more worthy of being followed, giving the section's guide-who-goes-ahead an explicit follower relation.
`وَلِكُلِّ قَوْمٍ هَادٍ` makes a guide belong to every people, linking a guide in front with the communal character of the path.
Pharaoh `يَقْدُمُ قَوْمَهُ` and brings them to the Fire; the leader who goes before is a dark reversal of the hādī who leads a people home.
Pharaoh led his people astray and `مَا هَدَىٰ`, naming the failed leader of a community as the opposite of the guiding one.
The believing man says, `اتَّبِعُونِ أَهْدِكُمْ سَبِيلَ الرَّشَادِ`: followers are invited behind a speaker who will lead them to the way of right conduct.
The next appeal contrasts his call to salvation with their call to the Fire, supplying the opposed destinations to the guidance in 40:38.
Whoever follows divine guidance will neither go astray nor suffer; following and not becoming `ضَلَّ` define remaining on the course.
The final question asks who are companions of `الصِّرَاطِ السَّوِيِّ` and who is guided, directly coupling the even road and hidayah.
The contrast is between one walking fallen on his face and one walking upright on a straight road, a bodily image of walking and orientation on `صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ`.
`اسْتَقَامُوا عَلَى الطَّرِيقَةِ` makes continuing steadfastly on a way the condition for abundant provision, joining straight continuance with the sustaining ground of the path.
Holding fast to God results in being guided `إِلَىٰ صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ`, naming how a traveller is kept on the road.
Obedience to God and the Messenger is answered with guidance to `صِرَاطًا مُّسْتَقِيمًا`, so the guide and the walked course are joined.
Those who obey join the people upon whom God has bestowed favour, `أَنْعَمَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِم`; it identifies the blessed company named as the road's people in 1:7.
Turning aside from the Messenger and following a course other than `سَبِيلِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ` makes the believers' way a communal route with a grave contrary direction.
Those who believe and hold fast are guided toward God on `صِرَاطًا مُّسْتَقِيمًا`; the path is explicitly oriented toward its destination.
Breaking the covenant is described as `ضَلَّ سَوَاءَ السَّبِيلِ`, another exact loss of the middle/even way.
By the Book God guides seekers of His approval to `سُبُلَ السَّلَامِ`; guidance supplies several routes whose end is peace.
The condemned are `أَضَلُّ عَن سَوَاءِ السَّبِيلِ`, using the even road as the measure from which a way can be lost.
People who went astray and led many astray have strayed from `سَوَاءِ السَّبِيلِ`, a collective version of departure from the road's middle.
Chosen ancestors, descendants, and brothers are guided to a straight path, furnishing a line of prior walkers for the communal path.
After the guided prophets are named, the Messenger is told to follow `هُدَاهُمْ`; guidance is received by following those who went before.
`هَٰذَا صِرَاطُ رَبِّكَ مُسْتَقِيمًا` identifies the Lord's road as straight after distinguishing the guided from the straying.
`دَارُ السَّلَامِ` is theirs with their Lord, completing the preceding Lord's path with the home to which that protected guidance belongs.
The people of the Garden say God guided them `لِهَٰذَا`; arrival in the garden gives the guided path its reached destination.
Those who reject signs do not take the way of right conduct even when they see it, but take the way of error; sight of two roads still requires right orientation.
Moses and Aaron are commanded `فَاسْتَقِيمَا` and not to follow the way of the unknowing, making steadfast progress and a contrary trail explicit.
`فَاسْتَقِمْ كَمَا أُمِرْتَ` commands the Prophet and those who turned with him to remain straight, giving the route its continuing communal practice.
Worship of God is called `الدِّينُ الْقَيِّمُ`; it ties the section's worship, religion, and uprightness together without separating them.
`هَٰذِهِ سَبِيلِي` is a proclaimed way to God shared by the speaker and those who follow him, a guide and a company on one route.
The Book brings people from darkness into light by their Lord's permission, `إِلَىٰ صِرَاطِ الْعَزِيزِ الْحَمِيدِ`, a passage led toward God.
The messengers say God has guided them to their `سُبُلَنَا`; divine guidance is described as a way on which they can rely and endure.
`هَٰذَا صِرَاطٌ عَلَيَّ مُسْتَقِيمٌ` names a straight path directed to God, sharpening the section's claim that knowing a road includes knowing where it reaches.
Each community receives the command to worship God and shun false gods; some are guided and others deserve error, joining worship to the hidayah/dalal divide.
Abraham is grateful for divine favours, chosen, and guided to a straight path; a blessed forebear becomes a prior walker on that way.
The Messenger is commanded to call to the way of his Lord, while God knows who has strayed from it and who is guided.
Abraham asks his father to follow him so that he may guide him to `صِرَاطٍ سَوِيٍّ`, a guide addressing a particular traveller.
Abraham's household are made leaders who guide by God's command; their exemplary guidance joins a people with leaders who go before them.
They are guided to good speech and to `صِرَاطِ الْحَمِيدِ`, so the same hidayah reaches a named path of God.
God guides believers to a straight path after they recognize the revelation as truth, making the path a response to received guidance.
The Messenger's call is explicitly `إِلَىٰ صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ`, a voice inviting hearers onto the route.
Those who reject the hereafter are `لَنَاكِبُونَ عَنِ الصِّرَاطِ`, turning away from the path just named in 23:73.
God guides whom He wills to a straight path after sending clarifying signs, joining signs and route-finding.
Those who strive are guided to God's `سُبُلَنَا`; the plural ways are paths opened by sustained walking rather than an abstract fact alone.
From among them God made leaders guiding by His command when they were patient and certain, a communal line of guides ahead of others.
The followers say their leaders and great ones led them astray `عَنِ السَّبِيلِ`, the inverse of following a hādī on the road.
The revealed Book guides `إِلَىٰ صِرَاطِ الْعَزِيزِ الْحَمِيدِ`, uniting scripture, guidance, and a destination-bearing path.
The Messenger is declared to be upon a straight path; his standing on it gives the requesting community a guide already on the road.
`اتَّبِعُوا مَن لَّا يَسْأَلُكُمْ أَجْرًا وَهُم مُّهْتَدُونَ` gives a concrete rule for choosing whom to follow: the guides are themselves guided.
The Prophet is told, `وَإِنَّكَ لَتَهْدِي إِلَىٰ صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ`, explicitly casting him as one who guides others toward the straight route.
The next ayah names that route `صِرَاطِ اللَّهِ`, completing 42:52 by identifying the road's owner and end.
Holding fast to revelation is paired with being on a straight path, showing how one stays rather than leaves the course.
The Prophet is placed upon a `شَرِيعَةٍ` and told to follow it rather than the desires of the unknowing, a prescribed course with a contrary divergence.
The Quran guides to truth and `إِلَىٰ طَرِيقٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ`, another direct union of revealed guide and straight way.
The jinn hear a Quran that guides `إِلَى الرُّشْدِ`; the response is belief, making the Book a guide toward right direction.
God has guided the human being to `السَّبِيلَ`, after which gratitude and ingratitude divide the response to that shown way.
`وَهَدَيْنَاهُ النَّجْدَيْنِ` portrays guidance as showing two rising ways, making a route visible as a choice with divergent outcomes.
They are commanded to worship God with sincere religion, `ذَٰلِكَ دِينُ الْقَيِّمَةِ`; worship and upright religion recur as the path's inner practice.
In the change of prayer direction, God guides whom He wills to a straight path, placing guidance within a scene of communal orientation.
The community is made `أُمَّةً وَسَطًا`; its middle position gives a social counterpart to the section's insistence on staying in the middle of the road.
People insist on what they found their fathers upon even when those fathers neither understood nor were guided, warning that a well-worn inherited practice need not be a true route.
The community is told to enter wholly and not follow Satan's `خُطُوَات`; communal wholeness is set against taking the adversary's footsteps.
Those who follow guidance sent from God need not fear or grieve, giving the prayer for guidance the character of a path to safety.
People who turn believers from God's way and seek it `عِوَجًا` oppose the straight line of the requested path by trying to bend it.
Holding together to God's rope and not becoming divided gives the one shared course a communal form opposed to scattering.
Some call unbelievers `أَهْدَىٰ سَبِيلًا`; the claim provides a false assessment of which way is more rightly guided.
The appeal to what fathers were found doing persists even when they lacked knowledge and guidance, another boundary on treating habitual tracks as reliable.
The believer is told that those who have strayed cannot harm them if they are guided, keeping the guided traveller distinct from surrounding wanderers.
God may leave one to stray or put one on a straight path; the exact alternative makes hidayah and dalal two opposed directions.
One party is guided while another's error is due; the latter take devils as allies and think themselves guided, an account of misoriented walkers.
Wrongdoers bar people from God's way and seek it crooked, a direct contrary action to guiding someone along a straight road.
A community guides by truth and acts justly by it, showing a people that carries guidance together rather than merely receiving it.
Whomever God leaves astray has no guide, making the absence of a hādī the condition of wandering.
Their Lord guides believers by their faith and they arrive amid the rivers of bliss; guidance here has the Garden as its reached dwelling.
After truth there is only `الضَّلَالُ`, a stark directional boundary that clarifies why the prayer refuses the state of the lost.
Those who bar from God's path and seek crookedness make the road's straightness an object of active opposition.
`إِنَّ رَبِّي عَلَىٰ صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ` makes the Lord's rule itself a straight course, grounding the traveller's road in divine constancy.
Satan is denied authority over God's devoted servants, completing the straight-path declaration in 15:41 with a boundary against the tempter's claim.
The one who commands justice and is on a straight path contrasts with a dependent person who brings no good, giving uprightness a guiding public speech.
The Quran guides to what is `أَقْوَمُ`, extending the section's straightness root from the road to the Book's most upright direction.
One blind in this life is more astray from the way in the next; lost direction is pictured as an inability to see the route.
Whomever God guides is guided, and one left astray finds no guiding protector; a guide's absence is linked to being lost.
Moses asks to follow a servant so he may be taught `رُشْدًا`; the scene concretely pairs a follower with a teacher who can lead him rightly.
Whoever takes Satan as ally is led astray and then guided to the punishment of the Blaze, a counter-guidance with the wrong end.
God guides whom He wills to a straight path through clear verses, connecting disclosed signs to route-finding.
Pilgrims come on foot and on lean mounts from every deep mountain pass to the House, giving road-walking a shared destination.
The Prophet is told to call to his Lord while being upon straight guidance, making his address an invitation from a sure course.
Obedience to the Messenger yields guidance, identifying following the one sent ahead as the way to be guided.
Whoever wills may take a way to his Lord; the road is explicitly an approach toward its divine destination.
At the sea Moses says his Lord is with him and will guide him, a traveller's assurance at a blocked route.
Satan has barred a people from the way, so they are not guided; their worship is a concrete rival route to worship on the straight path.
One who follows desire without guidance from God is called most astray, opposing a shown road to self-directed drift.
Turning one's face toward the upright religion, `الدِّينُ الْقَيِّمُ`, gives religion the directed and upright stance heard in the path image.
Those who split their religion into factions turn habitual religion into scattered parties, the social contrary to one walked road.
One who submits to God and does good has grasped the firmest handhold, a concrete image of being kept secure on the directed course.
The speaker sets guidance against manifest error between two parties, preserving the path's decisive fork even without a named road.
The arrogant ask whether they prevented followers from guidance after it came; guidance can be obstructed by leaders who redirect a group.
The command for criminals to separate begins the nearby scene in which worship, straight path, and mass misguidance are distinguished.
`أَلَمْ أَعْهَدْ إِلَيْكُمْ ... أَن لَّا تَعْبُدُوا الشَّيْطَانَ` supplies the opposite worship immediately before worship of God is named the straight path.
Those who avoid false gods and turn to God receive good news, a movement away from the false worship opposed to the path of worship.
Those who listen and follow the best of speech are the ones God has guided, giving guidance the form of attentive following.
The believing man fears that Pharaoh may cause corruption or make the people's religion prevail; within the later speech he offers a competing road of right conduct.
Thamud were offered guidance but preferred blindness to it, a deliberate exchange of seeing the route for losing it.
Those who say God is Lord and then remain steadfast (`اسْتَقَامُوا`) are met by angels, making continuance an enduring communal stance.
Communities are told to establish religion and not divide in it; daily religion is kept from becoming the scattered groups opposed to one way.
A people claim to be guided while following the `آثَار` of their ancestors, a critical counterpart to a path marked by earlier feet.
The same ancestral `آثَار` are named as the tracks a community imitates, continuing the question of whether inherited traces truly guide.
The messenger asks whether a more guided way than the fathers' way would still be refused, exposing inherited route-following as a possible error.
Devils bar people from the way while the people think themselves guided, a concentrated image of confident misorientation.
One who makes desire a god is left astray despite knowledge; worshiping desire reverses the worship-path ordered in the section.
Those who affirm God and then remain steadfast are promised no fear or grief, giving `اسْتَقَامُوا` the continuing shape of the straight course.
God increases those who are guided in guidance and gives them their mindfulness, depicting the path as a course whose clarity can grow.
Those who turn back after guidance has become clear abandon a course once shown, a temporal reverse of continuing without deviation.
Desires and conjecture are followed although guidance has come from the Lord, contrasting self-chosen drift with received direction.
The jinn describe themselves as differing `طَرَائِقَ قِدَدًا`, a plurality of diverging ways that makes 6:153's one path and many paths audible.
Those who submit have sought right conduct, while the unjust become fuel for Hell; communal direction has divergent ends.
The reminder is followed by the invitation for whoever wills to take a way to his Lord, an explicit route toward God.
Whoever wills may take a way to his Lord, again making the goal of guidance a destination rather than information alone.
`إِنَّ عَلَيْنَا لَلْهُدَىٰ` assigns guidance to God, supporting the prayer's direct address for leading.
The Book is `قَيِّمًا` and free of `عِوَجًا`; by an explicit bridge, its upright, unbent speech parallels the section's straight-line account of `مُسْتَقِيم`.
An Arabic Quran without crookedness is described as a means of mindfulness; its absence of `عِوَج` gives a textual counterpart to an unbent course.
God promises to guide believers to the `سُنَنَ الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِكُمْ`; the path is a way already travelled by earlier communities.
Moses and his companion return `عَلَىٰ آثَارِهِمَا` after losing their way to the meeting-place, an actual recovery of route by retracing footprints.
Moses is told to lead God's servants by night and make for them a dry path through the sea; a guide ahead of a people receives a traversable road at the obstruction.
`فَأَقِمْ وَجْهَكَ لِلدِّينِ الْقَيِّمِ` gives the upright religion the directed posture of a traveller setting his face toward a course.
David is told not to follow desire lest it lead him astray from God's way; just judgment is set on the side of staying clear of a diverted route.
The Messenger says the deity is one and commands, `فَاسْتَقِيمُوا إِلَيْهِ`; steadfastness is expressly directed toward God as the route's end.
The Prophet is told to call, remain steadfast as commanded, and not follow their desires, joining continued straightness to refusal of rival directions.
`وَلَا يَصُدَّنَّكُمُ الشَّيْطَانُ` warns against Satan's turning people aside immediately before Jesus states worship as the straight path in 43:64.
God's completed favour upon the Messenger includes `وَيَهْدِيَكَ صِرَاطًا مُّسْتَقِيمًا`, directly joining bestowed favour, guidance, and the straight path.
Believers are given a light `تَمْشُونَ بِهِ`; the image supplies illumination for walking, akin to the landmarks by which the traveller proceeds.
Moses asks Pharaoh whether he should guide him to his Lord so that he may fear, making guidance an address that leads a person toward God.
Different communities are given `شِرْعَةً وَمِنْهَاجًا`; this makes a boundary on reading every plurality of religious ways as the scattered roads rejected in 6:153.
Among Moses' people is a community that guides by truth and judges by it, a people that carries guidance together.
The foremost emigrants and helpers are followed by later people in good conduct, giving the communal path the human order of those ahead and those who follow.
Those who bar from God's way and seek it `عِوَجًا` actively turn the route crooked, directly opposing the unbent straight path.
After Abraham is named as guided to a straight path, the Prophet is commanded to follow his religion; a later traveller is placed behind that prior guide.
`الَّذِينَ أَنْعَمَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِم مِّنَ النَّبِيِّينَ` identifies the divinely favoured prophets whose company gives content to the people of 1:7.
`وَاتَّبِعْ سَبِيلَ مَنْ أَنَابَ إِلَيَّ` commands following the way of one who turns to God, then names the return to Him as the destination.
The command not to follow `خُطُوَاتِ الشَّيْطَانِ` makes Satan's preceding footsteps a rival trail across the earth's provided ground.
In the command concerning God's provision, people are again forbidden to follow Satan's `خُطُوَات`; a false leader's tracks oppose the straight path.
Following Satan's `خُطُوَات` leads toward indecency and wrong; the ayah makes visible why not every trail left before a walker should be followed.
